Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘following what came before.’ The expression occurs 758 times in 196 allowlisted texts and marks that a condition, action, or result remains unchanged. In encounter records a monk asks again ‘as before’ after receiving no answer, and a messenger answers Xuefeng ‘entirely in the same words as before.’ It also closes appraisals: ‘recognize it and it still is not it,’ ‘the blind remain blind and the mute remain mute,’ and ‘open your mouth and miss it; calculate and fail; still be embarrassed.’ A widely repeated three-stage statement says that after first seeing mountains as mountains, then not as mountains, one finally ‘still sees mountains only as mountains and water only as water.’ Verse and discourse also apply the phrase to recurring moonlight, spring, meals, and unchanged objects. The corpus supplies no specialized second referent: Zen bends this ordinary adverb chiefly by using it as the recurrent verdict that a new answer, recognition, or maneuver has left matters unchanged.
Senses.Note: Family check: compared standalone “as before” (依前) with “ask as before” (依前問), “the words as before” (依前語), “recognize it and it still is not it” (認著依前還不是), and “still sees mountains” (依前見山). These are deployment shapes of the same adverb, not different things; no sense split is warranted.

Senses.PreferredTarget: draw a gourd following the model
AlternateTargets: copy the gourd from its pattern
Senses.Explanation: Literally, follow (依) a model (樣) and draw (畫) a gourd (葫蘆). One master makes the wording concrete: after saying 'draw a gourd following the model,' he traces a circle with his hand and says, 'this is the model for the gourd.' Chan records most often use the idiom to appraise copied words or conduct in public exchanges. When a student repeats the form of an earlier answer, a master calls it drawing a gourd from the model and rebukes him. Another record explicitly denies that its handling of an old case is following another's heels or drawing a gourd from the model. A later address applies the phrase across famous lineage gestures: the Buddha holding up the flower, Bodhidharma facing the wall, Linji's shout, and Deshan's staff are followed by descendants who 'each draw a gourd following the model.' The Zen deviation is this ordinary craft-copying idiom used to audit repeated case answers, gestures, verses, and recorded lineages. Since masters also use it self-referentially, the phrase is not condemnation by definition.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 32 hits in 26 texts. One copying-action sense. Family checked against following another's heels (隨人腳跟轉), stamped from a printing block (印板上打來), released from a mold (模子裏脫出), and copying a model (依樣).

Senses.PreferredTarget: cling to grass and attach to trees
AlternateTargets: depend on grass and cling to wood
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “depend on grass and attach to trees.” Across 128 occurrences in 71 allowlisted texts, Chan masters use the phrase chiefly in the fixed labels “spirits that cling to grass and trees” (依草附木精靈) and “people who cling to grass and trees” (依草附木漢). Its targets are explicit and varied: making a livelihood on circumstances and objects or seeking clever explanations in principle and nature (機境上作活計，理性中求妙解), understanding under a “dead phrase” (死句), and even the stock teaching-seat actions of striking the bench, raising the whisk, blinking, and raising the eyebrows. The phrase therefore shifts from literal plant-dependence to a recurring Chan rebuke for speech, gestures, or understanding that depends on something named in the passage. The record itself supplies “spirit,” “person,” and the criticized dependencies; this entry adds no supernatural account.
Senses.Note: The construction modifies both “spirit” (精靈) and “person” (漢). Those are different bearers of the same predicate, not different senses of the headword. No plain botanical referent was established in the sampled Zen deployments.

Senses.Explanation: A sharp vocal cry: a shout. In Chan records it is a public-interview action available to both sides, not a sound reserved to masters. A master may shout at an arriving monk, a monk may shout and be struck, and the two head monks of Linji's halls shout simultaneously; Linji says host and guest are distinctly present in that encounter. Linji's record gives four explicit comparisons: a shout like the Diamond-King Treasure Sword, like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground, like a probing pole and shadowing grass, and a shout not used as a shout. When the monk hesitates over them, Linji shouts. The Eye of Humans and Gods later states that a shout distinguishing host and guest has host and guest within it and that a shout carrying illumination and function has both within it. The public interview also judges rather than automatically ratifies a shout: after answering a question on the great purport with a shout, Linji asks whether it was a good shout, and the exchange continues through fault and repeated offense. Another instruction expressly tells the assembly not to shout blindly or shout at random. A recorded shout can have an immediate bodily effect—after Mazu's shout, Baizhang is said to have been deaf for three days—but the corpus does not assign that effect or any one result to every shout. The act also closes teaching-seat speech in the stage direction “shouted once and left the seat,” and lists of house devices pair Linji's shout with Deshan's staff. The ordinary baseline remains audible in the Puhua episode, where an officer cries out to clear the road and Puhua also cries out while making a wrestling gesture. These are all the same vocal act in different institutions and sentence positions. The longer compounds “cheer” (喝采), “shout abuse” (喝罵), and “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) must be translated as compounds; no allowlisted drinking use was established.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count at the depth audit: 35,032 hits in 411 texts. High-frequency families include “one shout” (一喝), “shout once” (喝一喝), “the master then shouted” (師便喝), “the monk then shouted” (僧便喝), “four shouts” (四喝), “a shout not used as a shout” (一喝不作一喝用), and “staff and shout” (棒喝). The former entry's two senses—‘a shout’ and ‘to shout/cry out’—were merged because they paraphrased the same vocal event; noun and verb syntax alone did not establish different things. Targeted tests found no allowlisted drinking sense in “drink tea” (喝茶), “drink wine” (喝酒), or “drink water” (喝水). “Cheer” (喝采) and “shout abuse” (喝罵) are separately lexicalized compounds, while “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) supplies the ordinary calling-out baseline. Twelve witnesses preserve definition, master and monk use, simultaneous use, later systematization, explicit appraisal, warning against blind/random shouting, bodily effect, teaching-seat closure, house-device pairing, and ordinary road-clearing use without padding duplicate shouts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “shout one shout,” this is the records' stock narrative formula for a master's or monk's performed shout. In a public interview it can answer another shout: Muzhou says, “today this old monk was shouted at once by you” (老僧今日被汝喝一喝), asks what comes after three or four shouts, and strikes the monk when he has no words. Feiyin shouts amid a high-seat address and then says, “if I had not stopped it with a shout, this entangling talk would nearly have gone on without end” (若不喝住，幾乎打葛藤無有了時也). One record performs four shouts in sequence and follows them respectively with “the lion roars,” “the elephant king stretches,” “a mad dog chases a clod,” and “a shrimp cannot leap out of the dipper”; these are the record's four stated comparisons, not four dictionary senses. Elsewhere a monk shouts and exits, a speaker shouts before ascending the formal seat and offering incense, and another shouts before returning to the abbot's quarters. The same formula can close an address before leaving the seat, combine with planting the staff, or precede questions to the assembly. The Chan deviation is grammatical and institutional: a shout is preserved as a performed move within the public interview or teaching-seat event. This entry reports its position and any stated classification without assigning it an unstated force.
Senses.Note: The formula occurs 7,091 times in 320 allowlisted texts. Family comparison: “shout” (喝) can be a noun or verb, “one shout” (一喝) counts it, and “gave a shout” (喝一喝) is the finite narrative action. Speaker, addressee, and sequence position are different deployments of the same action, not different things. Compare leaving the seat (下座), ascending the seat (陞座), planting the staff (卓拄杖), and the abbot's quarters (方丈).
